# Hardware performs bi-linear interpolation of texture values [S3, unofficial]

The claim states that hardware performs bi-linear interpolation of texture values. The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly states under the 'Interpolation' section: 'The texture mapped slices are interpolated by the graphics hardware during projection of the polygon to screen space. Object-aligned 2D texture slicing requires only bi-linear instead of tri-linear interpolation...'. This confirms that the hardware performs bi-linear interpolation for the texture slices.
supported
Distortion artifacts if pre-computed slices are used for arbitrary viewpoints [S4].

The evidence explicitly states that when using pre-computed slices (which are orthogonal to a primary axis) for arbitrary viewpoints, the projection distorts the slice views, thereby degrading image quality. This is confirmed in both the notes and the passages, which mention that 'image quality suffers because the views of all slices will be distorted due to the projection onto the image plane' and reference Figure 4 illustrating this distortion.
unsupported
It is generally faster than software ray casting for large volumes [S2].

The evidence in Source [S2] discusses the performance of 2D texture mapping compared to 3D texture mapping (stating 2D is 'somewhat faster' than 3D). It does not mention 'software ray casting' or compare the speed of these hardware methods against software ray casting. Therefore, the claim that it is faster than software ray casting is not supported by the provided text.
supported

*   **Texture Memory:** Three 2D textures, each of size $D_x \times D_y$, $D_y \times D_z$, and $D_x \times D_z$ respectively, storing one copy of the volume for each slicing direction [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that three 2D textures are stored in texture memory, one for each slicing direction ($D_x$, $D_y$, $D_z$). The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly states: 'In contrast to 3D texture methods, three copies of the volume have to be stored in texture memory, one for each slicing direction.' This confirms that the evidence supports the claim.
supported
The approach was formalized by Cullip and Neumann (1993), Guan and Lipes (1994), and Cabral et al. (1994) [S3, unofficial].

The source text explicitly states: '2D texture methods traverse the volume using object-aligned texture slices [Cullip and Neumann 1993; Guan and Lipes 1994; Cabral et al. 1994]'. This directly supports the claim that the approach was formalized by these authors.
unsupported
Too large causes aliasing; too small wastes bandwidth [S3, unofficial].

The evidence supports the first part of the claim ('Too large causes aliasing') by stating that 'Lack of interpolation between slices may lead to aliasing artifacts if the scalar field or transfer functions contain high frequencies.' However, the evidence does not support the second part of the claim ('too small wastes bandwidth'). The text mentions that 2D texture slicing requires storing 'three copies of the volume' in texture memory (implying higher memory usage/bandwidth compared to methods that might not require this redundancy), but it does not state that making the slices 'too small' specifically wastes bandwidth. In fact, the text focuses on performance benefits (coherent memory accesses) and image quality issues (aliasing, popping) rather than bandwidth waste associated with slice size.
unsupported
Calculate the angle between $\vec{v}$ and the three primary axes of the volume data (normals $\vec{n}_x, \vec{n}_y, \vec{n}_z$) [S3, unofficial].

The claim asks to 'Calculate the angle between v and the three primary axes'. The evidence states that the base plane is determined by 'computing the minimum angle between viewing direction and face normals'. It does not mention calculating the angle between the viewing vector and the primary axes directly, nor does it provide a formula or method for such a calculation as described in the claim. The evidence focuses on finding the minimum angle to select the base plane, not calculating specific angles with all three axes for the purpose stated.
supported
# Interpolate in-between slices to eliminate popping artifacts [S3, unofficial]

The claim states that interpolating in-between slices eliminates popping artifacts, citing source [S3]. The provided text from Source [S3] explicitly states: 'Rezk-Salama et al. [Rezk-Salama et al. 2000] virtually eliminate popping artifacts in 2D texture slicing by interpolating and shifting inbetween slices such that the sample spacing along viewing rays is practically constant independent of the viewing direction.' This directly supports the claim.
supported
Interpolating in-between slices mitigates this [S3, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that Rezk-Salama et al. 'virtually eliminate popping artifacts in 2D texture slicing by interpolating and shifting in-between slices'. Since 'popping artifacts' are a form of visual artifact (the 'this' referred to in the claim), the evidence supports the claim that interpolating in-between slices mitigates this issue.
supported
Performance factors include software sampling rate, texture download rate, and polygon scan conversion rate [S6, book].

The evidence in Source [S6] explicitly states: 'The performance of this algorithm can be decomposed into the software sampling rate, the texture download rate, and the texture-mapped polygon scan conversion rate.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
Select the axis with the minimum angle to the viewing direction as the "base plane" normal [S3, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly states under the 'Data Traversal' section that the base plane is determined by 'computing the minimum angle between viewing direction and face normals.' This directly supports the claim that the axis with the minimum angle to the viewing direction is selected as the 'base plane' normal.
supported
1.  **Determine Slicing Direction (Base Plane):** Compute the viewing direction vector $\vec{v}$ [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the base plane (slicing direction) is determined by computing the viewing direction vector and finding the minimum angle between this vector and the face normals. The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly confirms this under the 'Data Traversal' section: 'the polygons are always parallel to the face of the volume data that is most parallel to the viewing plane, which is also called the base plane. It can be easily determined by computing the minimum angle between viewing direction and face normals [Rezk-Salama 2001].' The claim accurately reflects the method described in the evidence.
supported
*   **Gradient Storage:** Pre-computed gradients are stored in the RGB channels of the texture to allow bi-linear interpolation in screen space [S3, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the 'Gradient Estimation and Classification' section: 'Precomputed gradients are stored in the RGB channel and bi-linearly interpolated to screen space during polygon rasterization.' This directly supports the claim that pre-computed gradients are stored in the RGB channels and bi-linearly interpolated in screen space.
supported
*   **Popping Artifacts:** Sudden changes in slicing direction can cause popping [S3, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states: 'When the viewing direction suddenly changes from one slicing direction to another, the sampling through the volume changes as well. This may lead to popping artifacts, which are sudden changes in pixel intensity with changes in slicing direction.' This directly supports the claim that sudden changes in slicing direction can cause popping artifacts.
supported

It solves the performance bottleneck of software ray casting by projecting slices slice-by-slice, making it particularly effective for large volumetric datasets where 3D texture memory bandwidth becomes a limiting factor [S3, unofficial][S2].

The claim states that the method solves performance bottlenecks by projecting slices slice-by-slice, making it effective for large volumetric datasets where 3D texture memory bandwidth is a limiting factor. Source [S3] explicitly states that '2D texture slicing is still used for volume rendering today, and it outperforms 3D texture slicing for large volumes.' It explains that this method uses 'object-aligned texture slices' (slice-by-slice projection) and achieves higher performance due to 'coherent memory accesses' (addressing the bandwidth/memory limitation). Source [S2] supports this by noting that 2D textures can be 'paged in and out of video memory' to handle datasets exceeding video memory size, which addresses the memory constraints mentioned in the claim.
